title: Schools of Distraction abled-shortcuts/
author: Frederick Hess
summary: Hess notes a puzzle in public opinion: the broad turn against Big Tech has not reached the Chromebooks, learning platforms, and classroom software that fill American schools, where parental approval remains high. He offers two explanations, the standing appeal of future ready schooling and a default trust that educators are using the devices sensibly, and argues both are due for revision. The occasion is the Fordham Institute's new report by Brian Fitzpatrick, based on national surveys of 1,000 current and 1,000 recent high school students, which Hess reads as student testimony rather than abstract effect size. The numbers he pulls out are about time and evasion: most respondents spend more than half of class time on school issued devices, nearly a third spend more than three quarters, and three quarters admit daily illicit use of technology during school hours. On AI he emphasizes that students describe using it to avoid learning rather than to learn, with half reporting they have it solve math problems and a quarter using it during quizzes and tests. He highlights one finding as the most practically damaging, that heavier in class device use correlates with students believing absence will not affect their grades, which links ed tech to chronic absenteeism. His position is not that ed tech is bad but that it has rarely been used well, and his real complaint is that parents have not been angry enough about it.
points: Hess contrasts sharp public hostility to Big Tech with polling that shows most parents want the same or more technology in their children's classrooms.
The Fordham survey's core finding is one of sheer screen time, with 62 percent of students on school issued devices for over half of class and nearly one in three past three quarters.
Student reported AI use is overwhelmingly evasive rather than instructional, including 26 percent who use it during quizzes and tests.
A majority of students themselves say AI has made homework meaningless and lets classmates earn good grades without real work.
The report's link between heavy device time and the belief that missing school will not hurt your grades suggests ed tech may be feeding chronic absenteeism.
quotes: The pushback on AI and data centers is widespread and real, but parents seem a lot less worried about the devices that have overrun their kids’ classrooms.

Earlier this summer, EdChoice reported that 86 percent of parents support using laptops in class, 84 percent support the use of online learning platforms, 80 percent support the use of online learning games, and 60 percent support the use of AI in class.

Three-quarters of respondents reported using some kind of “illicit” technology daily during school hours—50 percent of respondents said they use social media (like TikTok or Instagram) at least once a day in school, 33 percent said the same about watching YouTube videos, and 17 percent about shopping online.

Sixty-two percent of respondents said they spend more than half their class time on school-issued devices. Nearly one-in-three students said they spend more than three-quarters of class time on screens.
Moreover, for all the suggestions that AI tutoring will bolster instruction, students are clear that they mostly use it to evade the rigors of learning.
Technology is fostering a classroom culture where students give the impression of learning while the school day becomes a shrinking circle of videos, memes, and chatbot-supplied shortcuts.
Here’s one very practical consequence: Fitzpatrick reports that students who spend more class time on devices are more likely to say that missing school won’t affect their grades.
The problem is that, in practice, 21st-century technologies have too rarely been used that way. I’ve long thought that parents should be angrier about this than they’ve shown themselves to be.
